prompt: A frame from a 35mm feature film, full-bleed, Chicago, 1928, night: looking straight up from inside a storm drain, through the cast-iron bars of its kerbside grate, crusted with coal grit and dead leaves. High above, on a stone balcony draped with limp bunting, a tall, skinny man in a bowler hat with a heavy gold chain of office round his neck, a long narrow face, hollow cheeks and a pencil-thin grey moustache, has just flung a handful of envelopes into the wind. The envelopes fall toward us. Press photographers on the balcony edge are firing flash-powder trays, and the frame is a stroboscopic multiple exposure: each burst freezes the falling envelopes at a different height, so every envelope leaves a ladder of ghost copies down the dark, and each flash comes through the red and blue bunting, staining its ghosts crimson, cobalt or bone-white. Flash smoke rolls in coloured clouds. At the grate's edges, hands in red scarves and blue scarves reach in, too late. The sky is starless sodium haze; the street is dry, gritty stone. The envelopes are plain and unmarked.
